summary: Bilge Yücel from Deepset introduces sovereign AI, defined policy-wise as an organization's ability to design, deploy, and operate AI on its own terms, and technically as explicit control over data flow, model choice, infrastructure, observability, and operations. She frames this around four pillars. Data sovereignty concerns where data is stored and processed—GDPR requires EU citizen data to stay in Europe, so sending it to a US-hosted embedding API already violates this; internal access permissions also matter. Model sovereignty is about controlling running models, training data origin, and having the freedom to switch models without architectural changes—tight coupling to a single provider creates availability and cost risks. Different models can serve different tasks: proprietary APIs for public data, self-hosted models (Mistral, Nvidia, Gina) for guardrails, knowledge bases, and LLMs. Infrastructure sovereignty spans a spectrum from air-gapped (EU AI Act safe) through private VPC (GDPR safe) and sovereign cloud to SaaS (Cloud Act risk). Operational sovereignty covers monitoring inputs/outputs, human-in-the-loop for high-stakes domains, and auditable versioning. Sovereignty is a spectrum—organizations must understand their vendor lock-in level. Retrofitting sovereignty breaks systems predictably: performance re-evaluation after model swaps, multi-database search routing after data migration, vendor lock-in exposure after moving on-prem, and black-box opacity when adding observability. Haystack mitigates several pains through consistent interfaces, explicit typed data flow, YAML serialization, and open-source transparency. A sovereign agent implementation is demonstrated: guardrails use an LLM message router to classify inputs as safe or unsafe; tools connect via locally-hosted MCP servers with selective picking and BM25 dynamic tool search when hundreds of tools exist; the agent component supports system prompts, local or API-compatible chat generators, and per-tool human-in-the-loop confirmation strategies. The full pipeline assembles a tracer, input guardrail, agent, and output guardrail. OpenTelemetry integration enables custom observability with all component inputs, outputs, and agent traces visible. She closes with a three-question sovereignty checklist: can you swap models without changing application logic, do you have reproducible run logs stored compliantly, and can your team respond to an incident without calling a hyperscaler.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Sovereign AI rests on four pillars—data, model, infrastructure, and operational sovereignty—each translating policy requirements into explicit technical controls.
Sending EU citizen data to a US-hosted embedding API already violates GDPR; sovereignty violations are often hidden assumptions baked into architecture.

Model sovereignty requires swappability without architectural changes; different tasks can use different models—proprietary APIs for public data, self-hosted models for guardrails and knowledge bases.
Retrofitting sovereignty breaks existing systems predictably: performance re-evaluation after model swaps, multi-database search routing, vendor lock-in exposure, and black-box opacity.
Haystack mitigates retrofit pains via consistent interfaces, explicit typed data flow, YAML serialization, OpenTelemetry integration, and open-source transparency.

A sovereign agent architecture sandwiches an LLM agent between input and output guardrails, with MCP-connected tools, BM25 dynamic tool search for large tool sets, and per-tool human-in-the-loop confirmation.
Sovereignty is a spectrum—organizations should understand their level of vendor lock-in rather than assuming maximum sovereignty is always needed.
Three questions assess sovereignty: can you swap models without changing app logic, do you have reproducible compliant run logs, and can your team respond to incidents without calling a hyperscaler.

sections.title: Introduction and Deepset Context
sections.summary: Bilge Yücel introduces herself as a senior developer relations engineer at Deepset, the company behind the open-source Haystack framework and an enterprise platform. Deepset serves large organizations like Airbus, Bosch, Siemens, and European public sector bodies, making sovereignty a core topic.

sections.title: Defining Sovereign AI and the Four Pillars
sections.summary: Sovereign AI is defined as an organization's ability to design, deploy, and operate AI on its own terms, translated technically as explicit control over data flow, model choice, infrastructure, observability, and operations. Four pillars are introduced: data, model, infrastructure, and operational sovereignty.

sections.title: Data Sovereignty
sections.summary: Data sovereignty requires processing and storing data within trusted jurisdictions. GDPR mandates EU citizen data stays in Europe; sending it to a US-hosted embedding API violates this. Internal access permissions—users seeing data they should not—also constitute a breach.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Model Sovereignty
sections.summary: Infrastructure sovereignty concerns where compute happens, spanning air-gapped (EU AI Act safe), private VPC (GDPR safe), sovereign cloud, and SaaS (Cloud Act risk). Model sovereignty requires freedom to choose and switch models without architectural changes and awareness of training data origin, though the latter remains unverifiable.

sections.title: Operational Sovereignty and Sovereignty as a Spectrum
sections.summary: Operational sovereignty covers monitoring system behavior, human-in-the-loop for high-stakes domains, and auditable versioning. Sovereignty is a spectrum—organizations must understand their vendor lock-in level rather than assuming full sovereignty is always needed.

sections.title: What Breaks When Retrofitting Sovereignty
sections.summary: Retrofitting sovereignty onto a working system breaks things predictably: swapping frontier APIs for self-hosted models forces performance re-evaluation and code rewrites; moving private data creates multi-database search challenges; replacing managed infra exposes vendor lock-in and hardware/network complexity; adding observability reveals black-box opacity and versioning gaps.

sections.title: Haystack as a Sovereignty Enabler
sections.summary: Haystack addresses several retrofit pains: consistent interfaces for cloud-to-self-hosted transitions, explicit typed data flow for traceability, YAML serialization for version control, and true open-source transparency without black boxes.

sections.title: Sovereign Agent Architecture Overview
sections.summary: A sovereign agent architecture is outlined: input guardrails check for prompt injection and regulatory compliance, an LLM agent with tools (API calls, knowledge base, sub-agents, MCP servers) performs work, and output guardrails enforce compliance. Haystack's role is ensuring everything is swappable, traceable, and free of vendor lock-in.

sections.title: Sovereign Agent Implementation in Haystack
sections.summary: The implementation is demonstrated in code. Guardrails are defined using a model provider (e.g., Nvidia chat generator) connected to an LLM message router that classifies inputs as safe or unsafe. Tools are connected via locally-hosted MCP servers with selective tool picking; tools can also be defined from Python functions or converted from Haystack workflows. A searchable tool set with BM25 provides dynamic tool search when hundreds of tools exist, avoiding context flooding. The agent component takes a system prompt, a chat generator (local on-prem or OpenAI API-compatible), tools, and per-tool human-in-the-loop confirmation strategies. The full pipeline assembles a tracer (with OpenTelemetry integration for custom observability), input guardrail, agent, and output guardrail. An example run pulls Q3 payment requests and generates a PDF. Different models can serve different tasks: proprietary APIs for public data, self-hosted models (Mistral, Nvidia, Gina) for guardrails and knowledge bases.

sections.title: Closing Checklist and Wrap-up
sections.summary: Yücel presents a three-question sovereignty checklist: can you swap models without changing application logic, do you have reproducible run logs stored in a complying way, and can your team respond to an incident without calling a hyperscaler vendor. She closes by inviting questions and social media connections for further discussion on agents, Haystack, and sovereign settings.

limitations: There is no reliable way to know which data was used to train a model, making training data origin a controversial and partially unsolved aspect of model sovereignty.
A good orchestration framework cannot solve hardware limitations such as GPU constraints when moving to self-hosted models.
Adding observability retroactively to a black-box AI system reveals that inputs, outputs, and intermediate states were never logged, making auditability difficult to achieve after the fact.
When an agent has hundreds of tools, filling context with all tool definitions is impractical, necessitating dynamic tool search rather than static tool listing.
